question: Which statement best describes SVG?
options: A `<title>` can provide a short name for a meaningful SVG, while a description can explain a complex graphic. This is like adding a caption to a diagram. Make the accessible name useful in the surrounding context. Do not repeat nearby text without adding information. For example, use a viewBox that includes the complete drawing so it does not clip when scaled. For example, a standalone chart needs a text description of its main takeaway.

`currentColor` lets an SVG shape use the element’s current text color. This makes an icon adapt when a theme changes. It is like using the same ink as the surrounding label. Set a visible color and check hover, focus, and disabled states so the icon remains clear. For example, currentColor lets a monochrome icon follow a button’s hover color. For example, set fill or stroke to currentColor so the icon follows theme text.

`viewBox` defines the coordinate space used by the drawing. It tells the browser how to map the artwork into the displayed SVG box. It is like the grid on a sheet of graph paper. A correct viewBox helps the graphic scale without clipping, so test the artwork at several sizes. For example, a chart may need a title and a nearby text summary of its important values. For example, a button containing an icon needs a name even if the SVG is decorative.

SVG elements describe shapes such as circles, rectangles, and paths. A path is a set of drawing instructions for lines and curves. It is like tracing a route on a map. Inline SVG is useful for icons and diagrams that need to scale crisply, but complex artwork may be easier to maintain as a separate file. For example, a small search icon can use a path and inherit its color from the button text. For example, use a viewBox that encloses the entire path to avoid clipping.
